source_text: Impune erratur, nisi delinquatur; quamvis et errare delinquere est. Impune, inquam, vagatur qui nihil deserit. At enim, si quod debui credere credidi, et aliud denuo puto requirendum, spero utique aliud esse inveniendum, nullo modo speraturus istud, nisi quia aut non credideram, qui videbar credidisse, aut desii credidisse. Ita fidem meam deserens negator invenior. Semel dixerim: Nemo quaerit, nisi qui aut non habuit aut perdidit. Perdiderat unam ex decem drachmis anus illa, et ideo quaerebat: ubi tamen invenit, quaerere desiit. Panem vicinus non habebat, et ideo pulsabat: ubi tamen apertum est. ei, et accepit, pulsare cessavit. Vidua a iudice petebat audiri, quia non admittebatur: sed ubi audita est, hactenus institit. Adeo finis est et quaerendi et pulsandi et petendi. Petenti enim dabitur, inquit, et pulsanti aperietur, et quaerenti invenietur. Viderit qui quaerit semper, quia non invenit. Illic enim quaerit ubi non invenietur. Viderit qui semper pulsat, quia nunquam aperietur. Illuc enim pulsat ubi nemo est. Viderit qui semper petit, quia nunquam audietur. Ab eo enim petit qui non audit.
thought_title: Seeking only belongs to those who lack or lost
orientation: Tertullian is answering the heretics' use of 'Seek and you will find' by arguing that seeking is only for those who do not yet have or have lost what they seek.
pass_a_gloss: One errs without punishment, unless one commits an offense; although even to err is to commit an offense. Without punishment, I say, he wanders who abandons nothing. But indeed, if I have believed what I ought to have believed, and I think something else must be sought again, I hope of course that something else is to be found, in no way going to hope for that, unless because either I had not believed, I who seemed to have believed, or I have ceased to have believed. Thus, abandoning my faith, I am found to be a denier. Let me have said once: No one seeks, except he who either did not have or has lost. That old woman had lost one of the ten drachmas, and therefore she was seeking: where, however, she found it, she ceased to seek. The neighbor did not have bread, and therefore he was knocking: where, however, it was opened to him, and he received, he ceased to knock. The widow was asking to be heard by the judge, because she was not being admitted: but where she was heard, up to that point she pressed. So there is an end both of seeking and of knocking and of asking. For to the one who asks, it will be given, he says, and to the one who knocks, it will be opened, and to the one who seeks, it will be found. Let him see to it who seeks always, because he does not find. For he seeks there where it will not be found. Let him see to it who always knocks, because it will never be opened. For he knocks there where no one is. Let him see to it who always asks, because he will never be heard. For he asks from him who does not hear.

choices.english: One errs without punishment, unless one commits an offense
choices.why: Keeps the impersonal passive force of the Latin, preserving the general statement about erring and offending.
rejected: Error goes unpunished unless it is a crime
It is unpunished to err unless one sins

choices.english: I am found to be a denier
choices.why: Preserves the passive of invenior and the noun negator, showing the result of abandoning faith.
rejected: I am discovered as a denier
I turn out to be a denier

choices.why: Renders the potential subjunctive as a self-directed statement, keeping the force of 'once for all'.

choices.english: Let him see to it who seeks always
choices.why: Keeps the future perfect imperative force of viderit as a warning, and the relative clause structure.
rejected: He who always seeks should look
Let the one who always seeks see

choices.english: up to that point she pressed
choices.why: Preserves the limitative force of hactenus and the verb insisto meaning to press one's case.

pass_b_english: Error goes unpunished only if no offense is committed—though to err is itself an offense. I say it again: the person who abandons nothing wanders without penalty. But if I believed what I ought to have believed, and then decide something else must be sought again, I am certainly hoping that something else will be found. I would never hope for that unless I had either not believed when I seemed to believe, or had stopped believing. So by abandoning my faith, I am found to be a denier. Let me say it once for all: no one seeks except the one who either never had or has lost.

That old woman had lost one of her ten coins, and that is why she was searching; but once she found it, she stopped searching. The neighbor had no bread, and that is why he was knocking; but once the door was opened and he received it, he stopped knocking. The widow was asking the judge to hear her because she was not being admitted; but once she was heard, she pressed no further. So there is an end to seeking, to knocking, and to asking. For it says, "To the one who asks it will be given, and to the one who knocks it will be opened, and to the one who seeks it will be found" (Matthew 7:7).

Let the one who always seeks look to it, because he does not find. He is seeking where nothing will be found. Let the one who always knocks look to it, because it will never be opened. He is knocking where no one is. Let the one who always asks look to it, because he will never be heard. He is asking from one who does not hear.
